articles.author: John NG
articles.description:
Just recently saw this post and decided that it would be interesting to test out Amazon Q CLI capability by building a game, so here we go!
First, I started by finding a game idea. Well turns out my high school teacher friend has some students find understanding physic concepts difficult, like free body diagrams. So I created this game for her students to understand the concepts easier~
With the game idea in place, I then proceed to setup the development environment and get my hands dirty. For anyone interested, you can refer this guide to install Amazon Q CLI.
Basically Amazon Q CLI is like ChatGPT/Grok/DeepSeek but in the form of CLI, so it's quite easy to use as long as you are comfortable with CLI environment.

So with Amazon Q CLI ready, now is time for prompting! It's working better than I expected as it appears Q is using a reasoning model by default, though the response time could be quite long as a trade-off.
Therefore, after endless prompting and revising, i find the below tips that maybe usefull in facilitating effective prompting and reduce the back-and-forth between you and Q:
Define a prompting framework such that the Q know the context, the task, and the expected results
Ask Q to provide visual debugs can let the Q know how to fix issues more quickly
Ask Q to give a plan before coding, that way you know Q is thinking as you expected
With about 3 hours prompting and waiting, here's the final product!

https://fbd.cmpapp.top
GitHub: https://github.com/john-ng-hk/stem-fbd-game
That's all and thanks for reading, feel free to connect me on LinkedIn too~
articles.title: Vibe coding a simple STEM Game with Amazon Q CLI

articles.author: Silvester Mugo
articles.description:
Microsoft Excel is more than just a spreadsheet application—it’s a foundational tool that transforms raw data into meaningful insights. From simple lists to complex data models, Excel provides a flexible environment for organizing, analyzing, and visualizing information across industries and disciplines.
 PivotTables: These allow me to summarize and analyze large datasets quickly. For example, I used a PivotTable to count product entries by rating category and discount level, helping me uncover patterns in pricing strategies.
 IF Function: The =IF () formula is incredibly useful for categorizing data. I applied it to group products into “Excellent,” “Average,” and “Poor” rating categories based on numeric thresholds, which made my dataset more meaningful.
 Data Sorting and Filtering: By combining Excel’s sorting tools with slicers, I was able to isolate top-performing products based on ratings, reviews, and discounts. This made it easier to create targeted visualizations and focus my analysis on what matters.
 Conditional Formatting: This feature highlights cells based on criteria, like coloring cells red for values below a threshold. It’s ideal for spotting outliers in financial data or tracking project deadlines.
Learning Excel has completely reshaped how I view data. What once seemed like overwhelming numbers in rows and columns now feels like a story waiting to be uncovered. Excel has taught me that with the right tools, I can dig beneath the surface of data to find insights that are not only informative but transformative. It’s made me more curious, more confident, and more equipped to approach challenges—one cell at a time.
articles.title: **_How Excel is Used in Real-World Data Analysis_**
